# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
Sections 1–5 do valuable, careful work. The overall conclusion does not follow from them. Their own best estimate is a gain of about +11% per actual hour. They then call the gain "entirely an artifact" on the strength of a novelty argument they never test, and they leave out the one randomised result that bears most directly on their claim.

## What holds up

I checked the arithmetic and most of it is right:
- Table 2: 95.1/0.8 is +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 is +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 is +10.8%.
- Hours: 40.3 → 34.6 is −14.1%; 40.4 → 34.8 is −13.9%.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 is about −2.6%.

The substantive findings are useful:
- **Attrition (§1).** If the microdata are right, the working paper misreported when and why organisations withdrew. Seven of nine left *after* the reduced schedule began, mostly over workload. That is a significant correction. It also lowers the continuation rate to 56/70 = 80%.
- **Output measure (§2).** Managers rated output above what their own records showed in 19 of 23 organisations. That is direct evidence of the rater bias that could previously only be suspected.
- **Hours (§3).** The time-tracking data quantify the scheduled-vs-actual gap. The resulting figure of about 14% is consistent with Varden's 13–17%.
- **Sectoral claims (§5).** The point that the per-hour metric mechanically produces "gains" is correct.
- **Data note.** It is commendably candid that the corrected subsets are not random.

## Problems

### 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own estimate
After the corrections, the best estimate is **+10.8%** per actual hour. That is smaller than reported but not zero. Moving from "+10.8% in a non-random subset" to "entirely an artifact" depends wholly on §6, and §6 says "six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one." Holding that the data can't distinguish the two explanations is inconsistent with concluding that one of them is the answer. "In our assessment" doesn't remove the contradiction.

The Data note also says the estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." Yet the conclusion extends beyond the pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.

### 2. The comment cites Varden selectively
It calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature," but never mentions Varden's other stratum. That stratum came from the same randomised trial, used record-based output and timesheet hours, and found **+12.5% per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4)** in case-processing at nine months.

That result was designed to rule out exactly the three artifacts the comment names:
- **Selection:** offices were randomised, not volunteers.
- **Measurement:** output came from administrative records and hours from timesheets.
- **Novelty:** the effect was still present at nine months, around the point where the comment's own extrapolation (§6) puts energy back at baseline.

The comment cannot accept Varden as authoritative where it supports their view and ignore it where it doesn't. A claim that gains are "entirely an artifact" has to account for this result.

### 3. The novelty argument is the weakest part, yet the conclusion rests on it
- **Energy is not output.** The decline is in self-reported energy, not productivity. The pilot collected the output index **monthly**, and the comment had the microdata, so it could have shown whether output per hour declined from month to month. That is the direct test and it is absent.
- **The extrapolation fits a straight line through two points.** It also doesn't match the stated figure. The fall from 0.61 to 0.29 over three months is about 0.107 SD per month, which reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten."
- **The burden-of-proof argument is rhetoric.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" can justify withholding a conclusion. It cannot justify asserting the opposite one.

### 4. The comment treats the meetings hypothesis inconsistently
§7 dismisses the Varden meetings correlation as post hoc and underpowered. Some of the description is also inaccurate:
- The seven offices are the **entire** treated case-processing stratum, not a subgroup "selected for analysis."
- Varden's authors themselves flagged it as unregistered and inconclusive, and registered a confirmatory test.
- The meetings data were collected in month six, before the nine-month results. "Selected… after the results were known" needs support.

The deeper problem is that the novelty account rests on weaker evidence: two time points of a self-report proxy, in a different study, with no output data. If n = 7 and an unregistered analysis rule out the meetings mechanism, the same standard rules out novelty as a conclusion. That matters because the meetings mechanism, if confirmed, would imply a *durable* gain. Both are hypotheses and should be presented that way.

### 5. The abstract overstates what was corrected
The abstract says the gain falls to 10.8% after "correcting the first three" problems, including attrition. Table 2 corrects only output and hours, and only within the 61 survivors. Attrition is documented but never incorporated into the estimate. The comment could bound it, for example by assigning the withdrawals worst-case or zero-gain outcomes, or by using Lee bounds. Until then, "four problems… account for most of the reported gain" is asserted, not shown.

### 6. The hours decomposition doesn't add up
The comment gives scheduled 32 hours, plus 0.7 hours × 4 extra on the remaining days (2.8), plus 1.6 hours on the day off, for **36.4 hours**. Reported actual hours are **34.6**, a gap of about 1.8 hours. Either a component is wrong or the figures are measured against different baselines. This needs reconciling, because the hours correction is one of the comment's two main adjustments.

### 7. Record-based output isn't automatically the true value
- **Billable hours** are listed as an output record. For professional services, billable hours mechanically fall when working hours fall. Using them as output turns "output per hour" into a utilisation ratio and biases the record-based index downward.
- Counts like tickets or cases closed miss complexity and quality. Managers may be capturing something real that the counts miss.

The 19-of-23 pattern is strong evidence of upward bias. But "records = truth" should be argued, not assumed, and the comment should report results by record type.

### 8. Smaller points
- **No uncertainty.** None of the corrected estimates has a confidence interval. With 17 organisations, the +10.8% could be quite imprecise in either direction, and that matters a great deal for the conclusion.
- **Uneven subsets.** Rows 2 and 3 of Table 2 use different subsets (23 and 27 organisations), so the "successive corrections" aren't strictly comparable step by step. Only rows 1 and 4 can be compared directly, with the subset caveat.
- **Retail.** The 11.2% figure for retail rests on three organisations.
- **Exit reasons.** Six said workload and two said scheduling. The ninth reason isn't given.
- **Revenue deflator.** CPI is a rough deflator for organisational revenue. The direction of the point is right, but output-price indices would be better.

## What the evidence supports

> Correcting for rater bias and actual hours, the Halden per-hour gain falls from 23.4% to roughly 11% in a non-random subset, before accounting for attrition, which likely biases it further upward. Whether the remainder is durable cannot be determined from six months of data. The only randomised evidence (Varden) finds a ~12.5% per-actual-hour gain sustained to nine months in case-processing work, and clear output and service losses in coverage-bound work.

That conclusion would be well-supported and important. "Entirely an artifact" is not, and stating it puts the comment's sound corrections at risk of being dismissed along with the overreach.

## How this fits with the other three documents

This comment confirms several problems I raised about the Halden paper with actual data: the withdrawals, the manager-rated index, scheduled vs actual hours, and nominal revenue. It also commits a mirror image of Halden's error. Halden treated its limitations as "unlikely to overturn the main result." This comment treats an untested hypothesis as overturning it. A correction can overshoot just as the original claim did.

I can draft a reply to the comment, suggest the analyses that would settle the novelty question from the existing microdata (monthly output trajectory, attrition bounds, results by record type), or write a short synthesis of where the evidence stands across the three papers.
